fact.box: FHSA to RRSP or RRIF (direct transfer)
fact.claim: You can put at most $40,000 into an FHSA over your lifetime, and no more than $8,000 in the year you open your first one. If you never buy a home, you can move the money directly into your RRSP or RRIF by the end of your maximum participation period, which is the earliest of 15 years after you open the account, the year you turn 71, or the year after your first qualifying withdrawal. Generally, a direct transfer does not use up your unused RRSP deduction room and has no immediate tax. This only works as a direct transfer with no excess FHSA amount: if you withdraw the cash and then put it into your RRSP, the withdrawal is taxed and counts as a new RRSP contribution.

plain.what: An FHSA is a savings account for a first home, and you can put in at most $40,000 over your whole life. If the home never happens, you can move that money straight into your RRSP or RRIF, which are retirement savings accounts. Done as a direct transfer, there is usually no tax right away, and it generally does not use up your unused RRSP room.
plain.so_what: If you take the cash out instead, the money gets taxed and then counts as a fresh RRSP contribution that can eat up to $40,000 of your RRSP room.
plain.do: Find the year you opened your FHSA and write down your deadline: whichever comes first, 15 years after opening, the year you turn 71, or the year after your first qualifying withdrawal.
